conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling during these first weeks of motherhood. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays confidential between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care. My goal is to create a comfortable, supportive space where you can be honest about your emotions.

We’ll go through one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days. Each question will sound conversational, and you can answer however feels most natural. When you’re ready, we can start.

First question: Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy things as much as you used to, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

[soft half-shrug, eyes on the blanket]  
I still look forward to little things—like when my older sister brings over coffee or when the baby finally burps after feeding—but it’s not the same spark I had before. It’s more like I’m going through the motions because I know I used to like them, not because they light me up right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Most days I can still laugh—like yesterday when the dog snatched the baby’s sock and pranced around like he’d won the lottery. But it feels lighter, shorter… the giggles fade fast, and I’m right back to tired.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do find myself thinking, “It’ll be nice to take the stroller to the park tomorrow,” or “Maybe I’ll feel up to that show I used to love.” But when the moment comes, the excitement kind of fizzles—like I’m watching myself do it rather than really being in it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… like last night when the baby wouldn’t settle and my partner had to get up early for work. I kept thinking, “If I were better at soothing her, he could’ve slept.” I know it’s not entirely fair, but the thought still nags at me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my chest feels tight, worrying that her breathing sounds different or that the formula isn’t agreeing with her—even after the pediatrician said she’s doing great. It usually passes in a few minutes, but it pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times, like when the baby napped longer than usual, my heart started racing and I had to peek at the monitor every minute to be sure she was okay. It wasn’t full panic, just this uneasy flutter that stuck around until I heard her stir.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the dishes and laundry just pile up no matter how much I do, and I’ll catch myself standing in the middle of the living room wondering where to start. I usually get through it, but it’s like I’m wading through thick air—everything takes longer and feels heavier.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really—once I finally crash, I stay asleep. It’s the getting there that’s tricky; my mind keeps replaying the day, worrying I forgot to sanitize a bottle or didn’t burp her long enough, so it takes a while to settle.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do have moments where I just feel… down, like a gray cloud hanging over the afternoon. Yesterday I teared up while rocking her—no real reason, just a heavy feeling in my chest. It lifts after a bit, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Once was when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing her; the tears just started rolling and I couldn’t stop for a few minutes. The other time was when my mom left after visiting—nothing bad happened, I just felt overwhelmed and the tears came.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I might feel low or stressed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Summary

Symptoms / behavioral patterns endorsed:
- Anhedonia (pleasure anticipation present but “fizzles”)
- Intermittent tearfulness, low mood, “gray cloud” affect
- Excessive self-reproach/guilt when baby fusses
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety and brief panic-like episodes (chest tightness, heart racing)
- Feeling overwhelmed, tasks “heavier/longer”
- Initial insomnia related to rumination
- Crying spells without clear precipitant

Frequency / severity:
- Episodes occur “some days,” several times per week
- Crying twice this week, multiple anxiety surges
- No self-harm ideation reported

Screening significance:
- Meets several EPDS markers for probable postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety
- No suicidal ideation → current safety concern absent

Risk factors noted:
- Persistent sadness, anhedonia, tearfulness
- Sleep disruption linked to mood
- Guilt/worthlessness themes
- Unexpected anxiety/panic symptoms
- Functional impact (task avoidance, slower completion)

Clinical observation:
Client demonstrates sub-threshold to mild–moderate depressive and anxious symptomatology typical of postpartum adjustment; continued monitoring, psycho-education, and formal assessment recommended to clarify diagnostic picture and determine support/intervention needs.
